For most of human history, the night sky was a shared inheritance: a band of stars visible to anyone who looked upward. That inheritance is quietly dissolving. The spread of electrified cities has scattered artificial light into the atmosphere, where dust and moisture scatter it further, producing a diffuse glow that astronomers call skyglow. Under this veil, the faint light of distant stars is simply drowned out. Surveys now suggest that a large share of people alive today have never seen the Milky Way from where they live, and that the brightness of the night sky over inhabited regions is rising by a few per cent each year.

The consequences reach well beyond stargazing. Many organisms time their behaviour by natural cycles of darkness. Migrating birds, which navigate partly by the stars, can be disoriented by illuminated buildings; insects exhaust themselves circling lamps; hatchling sea turtles, which instinctively crawl toward the brightest horizon, may turn inland toward roads instead of out to sea. In each case a cue that was reliable for millions of years has been overwritten by a human signal.

What makes light pollution unusual among environmental problems is how readily it can be reversed. Carbon dioxide lingers in the atmosphere for centuries; a poorly aimed streetlamp stops polluting the moment it is switched off or shielded. Lighting that points downward, that is no brighter than a task requires, and that is dimmed when no one is present can preserve both safety and darkness. The obstacle is not technical but a habit of mind that equates more light with more progress. Recovering the night sky, then, asks less for new invention than for a willingness to use, more thoughtfully, the light we already command.

**Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?**
option.1: Artificial light has now made it completely impossible for most people on Earth to see any stars at all from any of the places where they currently live and work.
option.2: The disorientation of migrating birds, circling insects, and stranded sea turtles is now the single most urgent environmental crisis facing the entire planet.
option.3: Light pollution is a serious but unusually reversible problem, and addressing it depends more on changing our lighting habits than on inventing new technology.
option.4: Astronomers, rather than elected officials, should be given final authority over urban lighting decisions because they understand skyglow better than city planners.

When a result in science is described as 'replicated,' it means that an independent team, following the same procedure, has obtained a similar finding. Replication is often called the gatekeeper of reliable knowledge, because a single study, however carefully done, can be misled by chance, by an unusual sample, or by an undetected flaw in its design. Only when a result reappears under different hands does the community gain confidence that it reflects something real rather than an accident of one laboratory.

In recent years, however, attempts to repeat well-known studies have frequently failed to reproduce the original effects. Several factors contribute. Researchers face strong incentives to publish striking, novel results, while careful repetitions of someone else's work attract little reward and are seldom published. Small samples can yield impressive-looking outcomes that vanish when the study is enlarged. And the freedom to analyse data in many ways allows a researcher, even unintentionally, to keep adjusting the analysis until a pattern emerges.

None of this means that science is broken. The very fact that the failures are being documented is itself a product of the scientific method turning its scrutiny on its own practices. Reforms are already spreading: some journals now invite researchers to register their hypotheses and planned analyses before collecting data, and commit to publishing the results whether or not they are striking. Others reserve space specifically for replication studies. What looks at first like a crisis of confidence may be better understood as a discipline learning, in public, to hold itself to its own standards.

**Which of the following best states the central argument of the passage?**
option.1: Scientific journals are the primary cause of unreliable published findings and therefore should no longer be trusted at all by readers.
option.2: Although many well-known studies have failed to replicate, this reflects science correcting itself rather than a breakdown of the method.
option.3: Small samples are, on their own, the single underlying reason that so many famous studies have proven difficult to reproduce reliably.
option.4: Replication is essentially impossible in actual practice because no two separate laboratories ever follow exactly the same detailed procedure.

A city map is never a perfect copy of the city it represents. If it were, it would have to be exactly as large and as complicated as the city itself, and so would be useless to a traveller. The value of a map lies precisely in what it leaves out. By dropping countless details and keeping only roads, rivers, and a few landmarks, a map becomes small enough to hold in the hand and clear enough to guide a journey.

The same principle applies to scientific models. A model of the weather, or of a population of animals, does not try to capture every raindrop or every individual creature. Instead it keeps the features that matter for the question being asked and ignores the rest. A model built to predict tomorrow's temperature can safely leave out the colour of people's umbrellas; a model of how a disease spreads can ignore the brand of car that infected people drive. Choosing what to leave out is not a weakness of a model but the very thing that makes it useful.

This has a practical lesson. When we judge a model, the right question is not 'Is it complete?' but 'Is it useful for its purpose?' A simple model that answers the question at hand may be far more valuable than an elaborate one that tries to include everything and so becomes impossible to understand. As one saying among scientists puts it, all models are wrong, but some are useful. Wisdom lies in matching the simplicity of the model to the job it must do.

option.1: Scientific models should always try to include as much fine-grained detail as they possibly can in order to be truly accurate.
option.2: Maps are, in the end, far more reliable guides to a city than scientific models can ever be to the natural world.
option.3: A good model, much like a good map, is valuable precisely because it leaves out details that do not matter for its purpose.
option.4: The colour of people's umbrellas and the brand of a car are in fact important variables in both weather and disease models.

**Read the following passage carefully and answer the question that follows.**

Before the middle of the nineteenth century, most towns kept their own local time, setting clocks by the moment the sun stood highest overhead. A traveller moving west by carriage might find each new town a few minutes behind the last, and nobody minded, because journeys were slow enough that small differences never mattered. Railways changed that arithmetic. A train that left one city at noon and reached another whose clocks also read noon had, on paper, taken no time at all. Timetables became puzzles, and collisions on single-track lines were a real danger when two crews disagreed about when a siding had to be cleared.

The response was not a government decree but a private one. Railway companies began publishing schedules based on a single reference clock, usually the time kept at their largest terminus, and asked stations along the line to follow it. Towns that resisted found themselves consulting two clocks: one on the church tower for daily life and one at the station for departures. In practice the station clock won, because it governed the arrival of mail, freight and visitors.

Only later did legislatures ratify what commerce had already settled, dividing territories into broad zones within which every clock agreed. The reform is often described as a triumph of science, and astronomers did supply the measurements, but the pressure came from the ledger rather than the observatory. What made local time intolerable was not that it was inaccurate; by the standard of the sun it was perfectly accurate. It was that accuracy of that kind could not be shared. A network needs its members to agree on a convention, and the value of the convention lies almost entirely in the agreement, not in the truth of the thing agreed. That is why the change, once begun, spread quickly: each town that joined made joining more attractive for the rest.

**Which of the following best captures the central point of the passage?**
option.1: Uniform clock time spread because travellers grew tired of resetting their watches in every town they entered.
option.2: Uniform clock time spread because networks needed a shared convention, not because local time was wrong.
option.3: Uniform clock time spread because governments saw that public safety required identical clocks everywhere.
option.4: Uniform clock time spread because astronomers at last produced measurements accurate enough to trust.

**Read the following passage carefully and answer the question that follows.**

Beneath the floor of most forests lies a dense mesh of fungal threads, thinner than hair and far more numerous than roots. Many of these fungi wrap themselves around, or grow into, the roots of trees. The arrangement suits both sides: the fungus takes sugars that the tree makes in its leaves, and the tree gains water and minerals that the fungal threads, with their enormous surface area, can gather from soil far beyond a root's reach.

Because a single fungus can be linked to several trees at once, the threads also form a route between plants. Experiments in which one tree is fed carbon labelled so that it can be traced show that a small share of that carbon later turns up in neighbours connected to the same fungal partner. This finding has been retold in popular writing as evidence that forests behave like cooperatives, with vigorous trees deliberately feeding shaded seedlings.

The evidence supports something narrower. That a substance moves between two organisms does not establish that either one intended the transfer, or that the recipient benefited enough to matter. Carbon may simply follow a gradient, flowing from where it is abundant to where it is scarce, much as water does. The fungus, moreover, is not a neutral pipe. It is an organism with interests of its own, and it may retain much of what passes through, trading resources on terms that favour itself rather than any particular tree.

None of this makes the network unimportant. A seedling that gains even a modest supply of minerals in its first seasons may survive a drought it would otherwise not survive, and that is a large effect from a small transfer. The caution concerns the story we drape over the measurement. Describing the forest as generous is a metaphor; the data describe an exchange whose accounting has not yet been done.

**Which of the following best states the main argument of the passage?**
option.1: Fungal links between trees are real, but claims that trees deliberately share food outrun the data.
option.2: Fungal links between trees mostly injure the trees, because the fungus keeps nearly every resource.
option.3: Fungal links between trees are so faint that the transfers recorded are probably measurement error.
option.4: Fungal links between trees prove that a forest works as a cooperative rather than as a competition.

**Read the following passage carefully and answer the question that follows.**

For much of the twentieth century, planners in growing cities treated the bicycle as a relic. Streets were widened, parking was added, and the space left for anyone on two wheels shrank to a painted strip beside fast traffic. Cycling did not disappear, but it became a choice for the brave.

In the last three decades many of those same cities have reversed course. The reason is mostly arithmetic. A lane of road carries far more people per hour on bicycles than in cars, because a bicycle needs about a tenth of the space and, when parked, almost none. Cities that could not afford to widen a single street found they could move more residents simply by changing what the existing width was used for.

Comfort turned out to matter more than exhortation. Where a city merely painted lines on the asphalt, ridership rose a little. Where it separated the cycle lane from moving traffic with a kerb or a row of parked cars, ridership rose sharply, and the new riders included many more children and older people. Surveys give a consistent explanation: most people are willing to cycle but unwilling to cycle beside lorries.

The change has limits. Bicycles work best for trips under about eight kilometres, so a city spread thinly over a wide area will always need other options, and hills and heavy rain reduce the numbers. Freight and emergency vehicles still need road space. What the experience of recent decades suggests is narrower than a slogan: for short journeys in dense districts, the cheapest way to add capacity is often to give a little room to bicycles, and the room only works if it feels safe.

**Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?**
option.1: Cities have returned to cycling because residents demanded a healthier way of travelling each day.
option.2: Cities have returned to cycling because protected lanes move many people cheaply on short trips.
option.3: Cities have returned to cycling because bicycles can replace cars on journeys of almost any length.
option.4: Cities have returned to cycling because widening roads for cars proved technically impossible to do.

**Read the following passage carefully and answer the question that follows.**

Economists have long treated their instruments as mirrors: a price index reflects inflation, an unemployment rate reflects idleness, a credit score reflects the risk that a borrower will default. The metaphor is convenient and, within limits, harmless. It becomes misleading the moment a measure acquires an audience. Once a credit score governs access to a mortgage, borrowers begin to manage the score rather than the prudence it was built to detect; lenders, in turn, price loans off the managed score. What began as a description of behaviour becomes one of the pressures that shape it. The measure is not merely inaccurate; it is productive.

It is tempting to read this as an indictment of quantification, and some critics do. The inference is too quick. Nothing in the argument shows that unmeasured judgment is more faithful to the world; loan officers working on intuition were biased in ways no one audited, and their errors, being invisible, were also uncorrectable. What the argument establishes is narrower and more awkward: the accuracy of a social measure is not a fixed property of the measure but a function of how consequential it has been allowed to become. A statistic used only by researchers may describe reasonably well what it claims to describe. The same statistic, once written into a contract or a regulation, begins to erode its own validity, and does so at a rate that has little to do with the care taken in its construction.

This has an uncomfortable corollary for institutional design. If validity decays with use, then the standard remedy, refining the metric, addresses the wrong variable. Better specification may buy time; it cannot arrest the process, because the process is driven not by measurement error but by the incentives that consequence creates. The alternatives are unattractive in different ways: rotate metrics before they are gamed, and lose comparability across periods; keep several imperfect indicators in play, and abandon the crisp accountability a single number provides; or make the metric one input among several to a judgment that remains discretionary, and therefore hard to challenge. None of these is a solution. Each is a choice about which kind of failure a system prefers to live with.

**The passage is primarily concerned with establishing which of the following?**
option.1: Credit scoring shows how a poorly constructed statistic can end up distorting the very market that comes to depend on it.
option.2: Because quantitative indicators are routinely gamed, consequential decisions are better left to experienced human judgment.
option.3: Social measures fail chiefly because those who design them pay too little attention to how the underlying quantity is defined.
option.4: A measure's validity falls once it is given consequences, so refining its design cannot fix the problem.

Nothing in the argument shows that unmeasured judgment is more faithful to the world; loan officers working on intuition were biased in ways no one audited, and their errors, being invisible, were also uncorrectable. What the argument establishes is narrower and more awkward: the accuracy of a social measure is not a fixed property of the measure but a function of how consequential it has been allowed to become. A statistic used only by researchers may describe reasonably well what it claims to describe. The same statistic, once written into a contract or a regulation, begins to erode its own validity, and does so at a rate that has little to do with the care taken in its construction.

This has an uncomfortable corollary for institutional design. If validity decays with use, then the standard remedy, refining the metric, addresses the wrong variable. Better specification may buy time; it cannot arrest the process, because the process is driven not by measurement error but by the incentives that consequence creates. The alternatives are unattractive in different ways: rotate metrics before they are gamed, and lose comparability across periods; keep several imperfect indicators in play, and abandon the crisp accountability a single number provides; or make the metric one input among several to a judgment that remains discretionary, and therefore hard to challenge. None of these is a solution. Each is a choice about which kind of failure a system prefers to live with.

option.4: slower in those cases where the measure has been constructed with greater care

**Read the following passage carefully and answer the question that follows.**

Reformers who export institutions tend to work from a plausible premise: if a commercial code, a bankruptcy statute or a securities regulator produced prosperity in one place, the same text should help elsewhere. The record is not encouraging. Codes copied faithfully have been ignored, applied selectively, or absorbed into arrangements their drafters never imagined. The usual explanation is cultural: rules that suit one society's habits will not suit another's. That explanation is loose enough to accommodate any outcome, which is a reason to distrust it rather than a reason to accept it.

A tighter account starts from what a rule is for. A rule does useful work only when parties can predict how others, including officials, will respond to its breach. That prediction rests on a stock of shared expectation built up through repeated enforcement, and such a stock cannot be imported, because it is not contained in the text. A transplanted rule therefore arrives without the very thing that made it effective at home. Whether it acquires one depends less on the fit between the rule and local values than on whether somebody with something to lose finds it worth invoking, repeatedly, before officials who face some cost for ignoring it.

This reframing has consequences. It predicts that transplants will take hold in narrow commercial domains, where a few well resourced parties litigate often, before they take hold in areas of diffuse benefit, where no single stake is large enough to sustain the litigation that generates expectation. It also predicts that the most durable transplants may be the least faithful: rules bent to serve interests that already existed get enforced, while pristine copies gather dust. Reformers who measure success by fidelity to the model will therefore misread their own results, treating as failure the drift that is the mechanism of adoption.

None of this restores the reformers' optimism; it relocates the difficulty. The obstacle is not that societies are incompatible with foreign rules, but that the asset which makes rules work is produced slowly, locally, and only as a by-product of use. Where no one uses a rule, no argument about its merits will make it operative.

**Which of the following comes closest to the claim the passage is defending?**
option.1: Reform programmes that export commercial codes to other jurisdictions should be discontinued as a matter of policy.
option.2: Bankruptcy statutes and securities regulation are the two bodies of law least suited to transfer across borders.
option.3: Transplants stall less from cultural mismatch than from missing shared expectation, which only local use builds.
option.4: Legal transplants take root only in those societies that already share the values held by the exporting country.

Options are usually treated as free, on the view that holding one costs nothing until it is exercised. In practice every open possibility levies a quiet charge: some attention reserved, some commitment withheld, some relationship kept provisional. The person who cannot choose is not made richer by the alternatives; the alternatives are consuming the very capacity that choosing would have released.

**Read the following passage carefully and answer the question that follows.**

For centuries, cartographers left blank the interiors of continents they had not surveyed, and some filled the emptiness with drawings of imagined beasts. These flourishes were not mere decoration. A map is a claim about what is worth recording, and the choice of what to include always reflects the purposes of those who commission it. A trade map emphasises ports, rivers, and the shortest routes between markets; a military map foregrounds ridges, passes, and the width of fords. Neither is a neutral mirror of the land, because no map can show everything at once. To be useful, a map must leave things out.

This selective quality is precisely what makes maps powerful and, at times, misleading. A traveller who trusts a road map assumes that the roads shown are the ones that matter, and rarely wonders about the villages the mapmaker chose to omit. When an authority draws a boundary as a firm line, the line can come to feel as solid as a wall, even where the ground itself offers no such division. In this way a map does not simply describe a territory; it quietly shapes how people imagine and argue about that territory.

Modern digital maps intensify the effect rather than dissolving it. They appear complete and objective, yet every one rests on decisions about which streets to label, which businesses to display, and which neighbourhoods to render in detail. The reader sees a clean surface and forgets the editing beneath it. Understanding a map, then, requires more than reading its symbols. It requires asking who made it, for whom, and what they had reason to leave in the blank spaces.

option.1: Trade maps and military maps differ chiefly because rivers matter more to merchants than mountain passes ever will.
option.2: Early cartographers decorated unknown regions with imaginary creatures to disguise the limits of their knowledge from buyers.
option.3: Digital maps have finally removed the distortions that troubled the printed maps of earlier centuries and travellers.
option.4: Maps are selective representations whose contents reflect the aims of their makers rather than a neutral picture of the land.

**Read the following passage carefully and answer the question that follows.**

When a forest burns, the loss looks total. Yet many woodlands have evolved not merely to survive fire but to depend on it. The cones of certain pines are sealed shut with resin and open only when the heat of a blaze melts that seal, releasing seeds onto ground newly cleared of competitors and enriched with ash. For such trees, a fire is not a disaster but the signal to reproduce. Ecologists describe these systems as fire-adapted, and they are far more common than the popular image of fire as pure destruction suggests.

The difficulty is that not all fires are alike. A frequent, low-intensity fire clears undergrowth while leaving mature trees standing, and many species are tuned to exactly this rhythm. When people suppress every small fire in order to protect property, dead wood and dry brush accumulate year after year. The next fire, when it finally comes, burns hotter and higher than anything the forest is built to withstand, killing even the trees that would ordinarily endure. In trying to prevent fire altogether, a policy can make the eventual blaze far more severe.

This paradox has forced a rethinking of how forests are managed. In several regions, foresters now set controlled burns on purpose, choosing cool, damp days when a fire can be kept small and contained. The aim is not to eliminate fire but to restore its natural frequency, so that fuel never builds to dangerous levels. The approach demands patience and public trust, since a deliberate fire is an unsettling sight. But it reflects a hard lesson: a landscape shaped by fire cannot be kept safe by pretending fire away.

**Which of the following best states the central argument of the passage?**
option.1: Foresters in several regions have recently begun to distrust the public's reaction to any deliberate fire.
option.2: Because many forests are adapted to regular fire, suppressing all fires can make later blazes more destructive.
option.3: The resin-sealed cones of certain pines will open only when a passing blaze first melts the seal and then frees the seeds.
option.4: Controlled burns should be set on damp days so that the flames stay small, contained, and easy to watch.

The public library began as a simple idea: that useful books should be available to anyone, not only to those who could afford to buy them. Early lending libraries charged a small fee, which kept out the very readers who might have gained the most. The breakthrough came when towns agreed to pay for libraries out of shared taxes, so that borrowing became free at the point of use. A reader needed only to live in the town and to return the books on time. For many families, the library was the first place where knowledge cost nothing.

Over time, libraries grew into something larger than shelves of books. **Read the following passage carefully and answer the question that follows.**

When we ask what a poem means, we are tempted to reach for what its author intended it to mean, as though the work were a sealed letter and criticism the act of opening it. The temptation is understandable, since intentions do govern most of what we make and say. Yet a strand of twentieth-century criticism insisted that, once a work is finished and released, the author's private aims cease to be the arbiter of its meaning. On this view the poem is a public object made of language, and language carries implications its user may neither have foreseen nor endorsed. A reader who recovers a documented intention has learned something about the poet's biography, not necessarily something decisive about the poem.

The argument is easy to caricature as a licence for arbitrary reading, but its careful proponents claimed no such thing. They distinguished the meaning of a work from the occasion of its composition, and held that evidence internal to the text, its diction, structure, and the conventions it invokes, constrains interpretation more tightly than any appeal to what the author confided in a letter. Where internal and external evidence agree, the appeal to intention is redundant; where they conflict, it is the text, not the confession, that the critic is professionally bound to honour. Intention, in short, is neither available nor desirable as a final standard of literary judgement.

Critics of this position have replied that meaning without a meaner is incoherent, and that to strip intention from interpretation is to reduce reading to the free play of association. The reply has force against the caricature but less against the original claim, which never denied that someone meant something, only that the someone's report settles the question. A more searching objection notes that the very conventions the text invokes are themselves the sediment of countless past intentions, so that intention returns, collectivised, at the level of the language itself. The debate, then, is less about whether intention matters than about whose intention, and at what remove, a competent reading is obliged to reconstruct.

**The passage is primarily concerned with:**
option.1: defending the claim that a reader is free to assign a poem almost any meaning that the language will loosely permit
option.2: tracing how twentieth-century literary criticism gradually abandoned nearly all close attention to the words on the page
option.3: presenting a view that denies the author's intention fixes a poem's meaning, and weighing the replies it draws
option.4: arguing that an author's stated intention is wholly irrelevant to every form of literary and biographical inquiry

**Read the following passage carefully and answer the question that follows.**

For a generation, the standard verdict on shared resources was pessimistic: where no one owns a pasture, a fishery, or an aquifer, each user has an incentive to take as much as possible before a rival does, and the resource is ruined by the sum of individually rational choices. The remedy seemed to follow with the force of a theorem. Either the state must regulate the resource from above, or it must be carved into private parcels whose owners will husband what they hold. Between the regulator and the auctioneer there appeared to be no third path.

Field research complicated the theorem. In mountain villages, coastal fisheries, and irrigation systems that had endured for centuries, users had neither nationalised nor privatised their commons, yet had not destroyed them either. Instead they had crafted their own rules: who could harvest, when, how much, and what would befall a cheat. These arrangements were neither spontaneous nor costless. They depended on the users being able to monitor one another, to communicate, to revise the rules as conditions changed, and to impose graduated penalties that punished a first offence lightly and a repeated one severely. Where such conditions were absent, the pessimistic prediction often held.

The lesson was not that the original model was false, but that it described one case rather than the general one. The model assumed users who could not talk, could not watch, and could not bind themselves, and for such users the grim conclusion does follow. Real communities are frequently able to do all three, and the capacity to make and enforce local agreements is itself a resource, one that erodes if outsiders, however well intentioned, override it. A government that replaces a working local arrangement with a uniform national rule may extinguish the very monitoring and trust on which restraint depended, and so produce the tragedy it meant to prevent.

**Which of the following best states the central argument of the passage?**
option.1: Communities can sometimes govern shared resources by self-made rules, so the pessimistic model fits a special case
option.2: State regulation from above is shown to be the single most dependable remedy for the overuse of any common resource
option.3: Traditional rural communities, unlike modern states, essentially never deplete the natural resources placed in their care
option.4: Shared resources are inevitably destroyed unless they are divided up into privately owned parcels by their own users

Rating systems promise to guide us toward quality, but a high average can mislead as easily as it informs. A product reviewed by only a dozen buyers may score higher than a rival reviewed by thousands, not because it is better but because a small sample swings more wildly. Worse, the people who bother to rate are rarely typical: the delighted and the furious speak up while the merely satisfied stay silent. option.3: People who feel delighted or furious about a purchase are much more likely to leave a review than those who feel merely satisfied.
option.4: Average ratings can mislead because small samples fluctuate and reviewers are unrepresentative, so a score reflects who rated as much as the product.

option.3: A breakthrough is frequently delayed by nothing more than a missing instrument or a question that no one has yet thought to ask.
option.4: Whoever announces a discovery first has often arrived only a few days ahead of several rivals working on the very same problem.

option.4: A rule that stays on the books without ever being enforced does not vanish but quietly remains available for later use.
